newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian stocks shrug off bank policy, await budget.
newsitem.headline: Indian stocks shrug off bank policy, await budget.

text.p: Indian stock markets on Tuesday shrugged off a six-monthly central bank credit policy designed to lower interest rates as investors stayed focussed on efforts to form a new government and pass a pro-growth budget, analysts said.
"At the moment it doesn't look like the credit policy will have a very big impact on the stock markets," said a strategist at a Singapore-based brokerage.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) governor Chakravarty Rangarajan told Reuters Television that capital markets would be boosted by policy announcements for the first half of 1997/98 (April-March) which allowed banks to invest more in shares of companies.
"Certain stipulations on bank lending against shares and investments in shares have been modified. All this will mean a boost to the capital market," Rangarajan said in an interview.
Bombay's benchmark index was steady after the announcements and traded 51.21 points, or 1.43 percent, higher at 3640.93.
Traders said news of a likely resolution to the ongoing political crisis remained uppermost in investors' minds, and the RBI measures were largely anticipated.
"The market is up on hopes of early end to political instability," said Sanat Dalal, a member broker at the Bombay Stock Exchange.
India's United Front coalition, backed by the Congress party's promise of support, was trying to form a new government under a new leader to replace the defeated Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
The centre-left government lost a confidence vote last Friday after the withdrawal of vital support from Congress, which wanted the alliance to change its leader as a condition for resuming support.
Traders said the market's key concern was the passage of the pro-business 1997/98 federal budget which has been held hostage by the political turmoil.
"It's a good credit policy but there are no surprises -- positive or negative," said Sandeep Dixit, banking analyst at Lehman Brothers in Hong Kong.
"In terms of increasing credit demand from corporates, the policy has built up on what the budget did," Dixit said.
The federal budget announced on February 28 boosted business confidence by slashing corporate and personal taxes across-the-board.
"If the budget does not get passed will we still see a pick up in demand for credit?" Dixit asked.
Parliament has agreed to take up the budget in a special session next week but it is still unclear whether the political crisis and amendments will blunt its thrust.

The RBI said in its policy for the first six months of 1997/98 (April-March) banks -- which previously invested 5.0 percent of incremental deposits in bonds, shares, debentures and preference shares of firms -- must now invest this money entirely in ordinary shares.
Banks could lend this money to companies against shares as the firms waited for capital to be raised through a public issue, RBI said in a statement.
"I think interest rates will come down, because the steps taken in this policy will lead to an increase in the lendable resources of banks," Rangarajan told Reuters Television.
The lowest prime lending rate among major Indian banks stands at 14.5 percent.
